assumptions: Let \(X, Y\) be arbitrary measurable spaces and \(\mu,\nu\) probability measures on them, respectively. Equip \(X\times Y\) with the product measurable structure.
mathematical_cores.boundary: The Lean conclusion is feasibility for the product law on arbitrary measurable spaces; it is not an optimal transport result. It does not mechanize the commentary about which assumptions are logically minimal. This is a narrow reconstruction of a real reusable local declaration, not a new Registry leaf or a formalization of the whole introductory coupling question.
mathematical_cores.context:
open MeasureTheory
namespace AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Measure.Transport
def IsCoupling {α β : Type*} [MeasurableSpace α] [MeasurableSpace β]
    (γ : Measure (α × β)) (μ : Measure α) (ν : Measure β) : Prop :=
  γ.fst = μ ∧ γ.snd = ν
end AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Measure.Transport
open AutoSamplingTheory.TechnicalLemmas.Measure.Transport
decoder_definitions: For a measure on a product of measurable spaces, fst and snd are its pushforwards under the first and second projection. The product measure assigns the product of the two marginal masses to measurable rectangles.

IsProbabilityMeasure is a Prop-valued typeclass stating that the measure has total mass one. IsCoupling γ μ ν is the conjunction of the two displayed pushforward equalities in the definition in the given Lean context.
mathematical_cores.difficulty_reason: The prose track derives the two coordinate pushforwards on measurable rectangles. The Lean track reads one coupling definition and recognizes the two directly applicable product-marginal identities; no measure extensionality or optimizer argument is needed.
mathematical_cores.lean_explanation: The task supplies the exact local IsCoupling definition, not the answer theorem. The existing proof uses constructor to split the two marginal equalities; simp then applies the Mathlib lemmas Measure.fst_prod and Measure.snd_prod. The first uses the probability instance for ν and the second uses the instance for μ. An explicit proof can use these lemmas directly instead of simp.

mathematical_cores.question: Show that \(\mu\otimes\nu\) is a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). Compute its two coordinate pushforwards, pointing out which of the two probability normalizations is used in each computation. Does this verify cost optimality?

rubric.criterion: Uses the two coordinate pushforwards as the coupling criterion, with the correct order.
Establishes the first marginal, using the mass-one property of ν (explicitly or by a correct standard product-marginal identity that identifies this premise).
Establishes the second marginal, using the mass-one property of μ (explicitly or by a correct standard product-marginal identity that identifies this premise).
Distinguishes the exhibited feasible coupling from a claim of optimality.

mathematical_cores.source_note: Original ASTIS exercise using the local product-coupling theorem (the feasibility witness for the Kantorovich problem in Chewi, Definition 1.3.1). It is not a copied textbook exercise. It shares the public coupling-swap-near-optimality family with the existing definition and mass-recovery items.
steps: A coupling has the prescribed first and second coordinate pushforwards. Both projections \(\pi_X,\pi_Y\) are measurable. It suffices to check the corresponding measures on every measurable subset of their respective spaces.

For measurable \(A\subseteq X\), the first projection has inverse image \(A	imes Y\). The product formula and the total mass of the second measure give \[ ig((\pi_X)_\#(\mu\otimes
u) ig)(A)=(\mu\otimes
u)(A	imes Y)=\mu(A)\,
u(Y)=\mu(A).\]

For measurable \(B\subseteq Y\), the second projection has inverse image \(X	imes B\). Here it is the total mass of the first measure that is used: \[ ig((\pi_Y)_\#(\mu\otimes
u) ig)(B)=(\mu\otimes
u)(X	imes B)=\mu(X)\,
u(B)=
u(B).\]
These two identities show feasibility. They contain no transport cost or comparison with another coupling, and do not verify cost optimality.
mathematical_cores.title: Constructing a coupling by taking the product law

case-1.assumptions: The only stated assumptions beyond the measurable-space structures and the types of μ and ν are [IsProbabilityMeasure μ] and [IsProbabilityMeasure ν], meaning μ(univ) = 1 and ν(univ) = 1. No topology, countability, or other regularity assumption is supplied.
case-1.conclusion: IsCoupling (μ.prod ν) μ ν, which unfolds to (μ.prod ν).fst = μ ∧ (μ.prod ν).snd = ν. Thus the product measure has exactly the two specified marginals.
case-1.constants: IsCoupling denotes the displayed conjunction of marginal equalities; Measure.prod denotes the product measure whose measurable-rectangle mass is μ(A) × ν(B); Measure.fst and Measure.snd denote the coordinate pushforwards. The numeral 1 is the prescribed mass of the whole space in each IsProbabilityMeasure assumption; no numerical tolerance, cost, or other parameter is present.
case-1.domains: μ is on α, ν is on β, and μ.prod ν is on α × β with the product measurable-space structure. The coordinate projections map α × β to α and β respectively. The measurable-rectangle interpretation uses measurable A ⊆ α and B ⊆ β.
case-1.objects: Types α and β equipped with measurable-space structures; measures μ : Measure α and ν : Measure β; their product measure μ.prod ν : Measure (α × β); and its first and second marginal measures.
case-1.quantifiers: For every pair of types α and β, with implicit measurable-space instances on each, and for every explicitly supplied μ : Measure α and ν : Measure β with implicit IsProbabilityMeasure instances for both. No separate measure γ is quantified in the example: the first argument of IsCoupling is fixed to μ.prod ν.
case-1.senses: The equalities are exact equalities of measures under pushforward along the first and second coordinate projections. On measurable A and B, the marginals evaluate the product measure on A × univ and univ × B respectively, yielding μ(A) and ν(B) by the rectangle formula and unit masses. The conclusion certifies this particular product measure as a coupling; it does not assert that every coupling is a product, that this coupling is unique or optimal, or that either projection pushforward equals its marginal only approximately or almost everywhere.
